case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress’s funding mechanism for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau—drawing money from the Federal Reserve up to a statutory cap rather than through annual appropriations—violates the Constitution’s Appropriations Clause (and related separation-of-powers principles), and if so what remedy follows for CFPB actions funded that way.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 7 (Appropriations Clause: “No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law”); plus the CFPB’s funding provisions in the Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (12 U.S.C. § 5497).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The CFPB (and the United States) argue that the Bureau’s funding is constitutional because it is an “appropriation made by law”: Congress itself enacted a statute that specifies the source (Federal Reserve System earnings), sets a cap, and controls the purpose and availability of funds; the Appropriations Clause restricts withdrawals from the Treasury and is satisfied by standing (multi-year or permanent) appropriations, which have been common since the Founding. Petitioners also contend the Fifth Circuit’s novel rule—treating certain non-annual, non-Treasury funding structures as unconstitutional—has no basis in constitutional text or history, would destabilize numerous long-established funding arrangements, and the remedy of vacating the payday lending rule is improper because the challenged rule was duly issued under statutory authority regardless of the funding mechanism.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The industry respondents argue the CFPB’s funding structure violates the Appropriations Clause and separation of powers because it (1) insulates the Bureau from the normal congressional appropriations process, (2) allows the CFPB to self-determine its budget within a broad cap set by reference to the Federal Reserve’s operating expenses, and (3) compounds insulation by routing funds outside ordinary annual appropriations and (as characterized by respondents) outside meaningful legislative control, thereby diminishing Congress’s core power of the purse. They maintain that this structural defect requires setting aside CFPB actions (including the challenged payday lending rule) that were promulgated using unconstitutional funding, and that upholding the scheme would permit Congress to evade appropriations constraints by creating similarly insulated agencies.

Collins v. Yellen (2021) (severability/remedy for structural constitutional violations in agency design)
Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020) (CFPB structure; separation of powers background often invoked in CFPB challenges)
Cincinnati Soap Co. v. United States (1937) (Congress may dedicate revenues via statute; cited in appropriations discussions)
Office of Personnel Management v. Richmond (1990) (payments from the Treasury require statutory authorization; Appropriations Clause principles)
United States v. MacCollom (1976) (appropriations and spending only as authorized by Congress)
Train v. City of New York (1975) (executive must follow statutory spending directions; congressional control over appropriations)

Justice Barrett’s reliance on OPM v. Richmond and Justice Kavanaugh’s point about the destabilizing implications reinforce that our precedents (including Cincinnati Soap’s “means simply” formulation) treat the Clause as a constraint on unauthorized executive disbursement, not a mandate for annual, line-item appropriations. To the extent there is any residual separation-of-powers concern, Justice Alito’s remedy point grounded in Collins v. Yellen counsels strongly against sweeping invalidation absent a concrete, traceable harm from the funding feature. A narrow holding upholding § 5497 as an “appropriation made by law,” without endorsing the CFPB’s design as optimal, best preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids constitutionalizing appropriations practice.

case_analysis.petitioner_position: The CFPB (and the United States) argues that the Bureau’s funding mechanism is constitutional because it is an “appropriation made by law”: Congress enacted a statute specifying the source (Federal Reserve earnings), the decisionmaker (CFPB Director’s request), and an upper limit (a cap tied to the Federal Reserve’s operating expenses). Petitioners contend the Appropriations Clause does not require annual line-item appropriations, permits standing and self-executing appropriations, and historically Congress has used many non-annual or dedicated funding models. They maintain that actions taken under this unconstitutional funding—such as the challenged rule—should be set aside.

Richmond, 496 U.S. 414, 424 (1990) (quoting Cincinnati Soap Co. v. United States, 301 U.S. 308, 321 (1937)), and it does not textually require annual or line-item appropriations. Cincinnati Soap further recognizes that the Clause operates as a restriction on Executive disbursement absent statutory authorization, not as a freestanding command that Congress must retain periodic appropriations leverage over every program. Because the funding mechanism satisfies the original public meaning of an “Appropriation[] made by Law,” there is no constitutional violation and no basis to set aside CFPB actions on that ground.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article I, § 9, cl. 7 requires that money be drawn from the Treasury only "in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law," and the relevant statute does just that by specifying the source (Federal Reserve earnings), the authorized recipient (CFPB), and an enforceable cap on the amount. As Richmond explains, the Clause’s "straightforward" demand is statutory authorization for payments, not an annual line-item appropriations process, and Cincinnati Soap likewise characterizes the Clause as a restriction on executive disbursing authority rather than a freestanding command about Congress’s internal budgeting mechanics. Whatever one thinks of the CFPB’s independence as a policy matter, the constitutional defect alleged here is structural and untethered to the Clause’s text; a holding otherwise would call into question many long-standing dedicated or standing appropriations schemes. Even assuming some constitutional concern, Collins v. Yellen counsels against automatically invalidating downstream agency actions absent a showing of compensable harm or a causal connection between the funding feature and the challenged rule.
